From: Samira Qureshi <samira.qureshi@healthhub.com>
To: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa.ortiz@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-09-05T08:14:00Z
Subject: Request: visualization of processing hops + subprocessor roster

Hi Vanessa,

Thanks for the intro last week — HealthHub is evaluating Redwood for a pilot and our security team asked for a concise visualization of where LLM requests are executed and which subprocessors handle each hop. Specifically they want:

- A diagram showing the sequence of hops from ingestion to inference to logging/metrics and long-term storage (if applicable).
- A roster of subprocessors mapped to each hop and the region(s) where they operate.
- Retention defaults for request payloads, embeddings, and audit logs plus deletion SLA for hosted vs dedicated/private.
- Any cross-border transfer controls and legal safeguards you rely on (SCCs, DPA terms, on-prem options).

Can you share a short diagram and a bullet summary? If possible include any export-control considerations for EU patient dataset processing.

Thanks — happy to loop in our infra lead if helpful.

Best,
Samira
Samira Qureshi
Director, Information Security
HealthHub

Subject: Re: Request: visualization of processing hops + subprocessor roster

Hi Samira — thanks for the clear list. High-level answers below and I attached a simple hop diagram and our current subprocessor roster CSV. See inline for the retention/deletion points.

1) Regions / execution loci (hosted defaults):
   - Request handling and tokenization: us-west-2 (primary), eu-west-1 (EU-serving tenants), us-east-1 (fallback).
   - Model inference (GPU infra): eu-west-1, us-west-2, asia-southeast-1 (for APAC customers).
   - Short-term KV/prefix cache & logs for routing: region-matched (same region as inference when available).
   - Long-term analytics/telemetry: us-east-1 (replicated), with EU-only replication available on request for customers requiring data locality.

2) Subprocessor mapping (attached CSV):
   - Cloud compute provider: AWS (EC2/GPU, region-specific) — handles model execution and ephemeral caches.
   - Managed GPU partner: Redwood Accelerator Inc. (dedicated pools; operates in us-west-2 + eu-west-1).
   - Metrics & analytics: OpenSight Analytics (us-east-1 by default; EU replication option).
   - Customer-configurable object store (for Dedicated/Private): S3-compatible or on-prem backing (customer-managed).

3) Cross-border transfers & legal safeguards:
   - For EU-hosted tenants we provision inference in eu-west-1 by default and keep telemetry in-region unless customer requests otherwise.
   - Where cross-border transfers occur (e.g., failover or centralized analytics), transfers are covered by our DPA which includes SCCs; we can also offer Data Processing Addendum with EU-specific terms.
   - Private deployments: customer-managed network and storage so no outbound transfers unless customer configures them.

4) Retention & deletion (hosted API defaults, editable via config):
   - Request payloads (transient): retained for 30 days for debugging by default, then purged from live caches.
   - Embeddings/derived artifacts: stored for 90 days by default if customer enables; otherwise not persisted.
   - Audit logs/metrics: aggregated metrics retained for 365 days; raw logs (for troubleshooting) retained 90 days.
   - Deletion SLA: hosted account-level deletion requests are processed within 30 days. For Dedicated customers we support contractually-agreed retention and deletion windows; Private deployments are subject to customer controls.

5) Export controls / sensitive data notes:
   - We recommend customers avoid submitting full patient identifiers in prompts; where required we can discuss a private deployment or stricter retention.

Next steps: attached are a lightweight diagram (processing-hop-diagram.pdf) and the subprocessor inventory (subprocessor-inventory.csv). Happy to run through this on a short call — proposing 45 minutes next Tue/Thu.

Regards,
Vanessa Ortiz
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference

Attachments: processing-hop-diagram.pdf (diagram), subprocessor-inventory.csv (CSV roster)

Vanessa — this is helpful, thanks. A couple of clarifying follow-ups from our infra/security review:

- Are embeddings generated for every request by default or only when explicitly enabled? If generated, where are they stored and for how long?
- For the request payload retention you listed 30 days — does that include the full prompt and user metadata fields (we need to know PII exposure surface)?
- For cross-border failover (e.g., eu->us during capacity events), does Redwood redact or pseudonymize identifiable fields before exporting, or are raw payloads transferred?
- Do you have a recent SOC 2-type report or a summary of audit logging we can review as evidence?

If you can add short answers inline it will accelerate our procurement conversation. We may bring our infra lead (Evan) into the call if needed.

Cheers,
Samira

Thanks — answers inline below.

> Are embeddings generated for every request by default or only when explicitly enabled?
- Embeddings are generated only when customers opt-in or call the embeddings endpoint. For customers who enable semantic features we can configure TTLs or a no-persistence mode. By default, if enabled, embeddings are stored for 90 days and are mapped to a tenant-scoped identifier (not global).

> For the request payload retention you listed 30 days — does that include the full prompt and user metadata fields?
- The 30-day transient retention includes the raw prompt and minimal routing metadata used for debugging (timestamp, tenant ID, request id). We explicitly strip known PII fields according to customer-provided parsing rules when configured; otherwise raw prompts are retained for the window unless the customer opts into reduced retention.

> For cross-border failover, does Redwood redact or pseudonymize identifiable fields before exporting, or are raw payloads transferred?
- In failover events we do not automatically pseudonymize. We rely on tenant routing policies — primary approach is to keep EU tenants in eu-west-1; cross-border transfers only occur for failover or centralized analytics and are covered by SCCs. For sensitive workloads we recommend Dedicated or Private to avoid cross-border hops. We can implement an additional pseudonymization step as a contractual engineering project if required.

> Do you have a recent SOC 2-type report or a summary of audit logging we can review as evidence?
- Yes — we have a current SOC 2 Type II report and an audit-log extract template we can share under NDA. I'll ask Marissa to coordinate delivery.

Next steps:
- I'll schedule a 45-minute walkthrough and bring our infra solutions engineer (Connor) to go through the diagram and any network details.
- Marissa will send the SOC 2 handover link and a sanitized sample of audit logs.

If you want us to produce a bespoke diagram that shows only EU-resident hops (no cross-border arrows) we can do that for the procurement packet.

Best,
Vanessa Ortiz
